tip: Withdrawing is 'lifting': σήκωσα πενήντα ευρώ (síkosa penínda evró) = literally 'I lifted fifty euros' – the everyday way to say it.
Cards 'pass': δεν πέρασε η κάρτα (dhen pérase i kárta) = literally 'the card didn't pass' – the standard phrase for a declined card.
You lift money from an ATM: σήκωσα λεφτά (sikosa lefta = I lifted money). Σηκώνω (sikono), the verb for picking things up, is the everyday word for withdrawing cash.
'Per day' has no 'per' – just 'the day': τη μέρα (ti mera). Rates usually work this way: δύο φορές τη βδομάδα (dhio fores ti vdhomadha) = twice a week.
Τον άλλο μήνα (ton allo mina) – literally 'the other month' – means next month, not some other one. Same trick: την άλλη βδομάδα (tin alli vdhomadha) = next week.
The word for 'it' comes before the verb in statements: την ακύρωσα (tin akirosa) = literally 'it I-canceled'. Only commands flip it: ακύρωσέ την (akirose tin).
Λογαριασμός (loghariasmos) is both 'bank account' and 'bill' – here τον λογαριασμό του ρεύματος (ton loghariasmo tou revmatos) is the electricity bill. Context decides which.
Μου έκοψαν (mou ekopsan = they cut on me) – no 'they' word appears. Greek uses a bare plural verb for companies and authorities; the μου (mou) marks who it hit.
Δεν (dhen) and τίποτα (tipota) stack: δεν μου έμεινε τίποτα (dhen mou emine tipota = nothing was left to me). Greek keeps both negatives where English drops one.
'Than' before a verb is απ' ό,τι (ap' o,ti): πιο γρήγορα απ' ό,τι περίμενα (pio ghrighora ap' o,ti perimena = faster than I expected). Plain από (apo) compares nouns.
Money 'enters': μπήκε ο μισθός (bíke o misthós) = literally 'entered the salary' – verb first, and the pay does the moving.
After a warning, μη (mi) attaches straight to the verb: πρόσεξε μη δώσεις (prósexe mi dhósis) = 'watch out you don't give' – no να (na) needed.
Δεν προλάβαινα να πληρώσω (dhen prolavena na pliroso) = I didn't manage to pay in time. Προλαβαίνω (prolaveno) packs 'have time to' into one verb – no 'time' word needed.
One verb, two directions: δανείζω (dhanízo) = lend, δανείζομαι (dhanízome) = borrow – the card's δάνεισε (dhánise) = he lent.
Saved money goes 'to the edge': βάζω λίγα λεφτά στην άκρη (vazo ligha lefta stin akri = I put a little money at the edge) = set aside. Greek's standard image for saving.
Μακάρι να + past tense = an unreal wish: μακάρι να μπορούσα (makári na boroúsa) = 'I wish I could' – the past form signals it isn't happening.
Μην + present forbids the habit: μην ξοδεύεις (min xodhévis) = 'don't be spending (ever)'. A one-off ban uses the other form: μην ξοδέψεις (min xodhépsis).
Τα βγάζουμε πέρα (ta vghazoume pera) – literally 'we get them across' – is the usual phrase for making ends meet. The τα (ta) points to nothing specific; it's baked into the idiom.
After να (na), 'not' is μη (mi), never δεν (dhen): να μη χρωστάς (na mi khrostas = that you not owe). Δεν (dhen) is for plain statements and questions.
Λεφτά (lefta = money) is a plural word: τα λεφτά δεν φτάνουν (ta lefta dhen ftanoun) – literally 'the moneys don't reach'. Its articles and verbs always go plural.
The school level takes the of-form: πρώτη δημοτικού (próti dhimotikoú) = literally 'first (grade) of primary' – no word for 'grade' needed.
Εσύ (esí) is optional since the verb already says who; tacked on at the end it points the question at you personally.
Δίνω εξετάσεις (dhíno exetásis) = sit exams, not 'give' them.
Περνάω (pernáo = pass) also means getting accepted: πέρασα στο πανεπιστήμιο (pérasa sto panepistímio) = I got into university.
Φροντιστήριο (frontistírio) = private cram school, near-universal before the exams.
Διαβάζω (dhiavázo) means both 'read' and 'study'; context tells them apart.
Το πρωί (to proí) = in the morning; parts of the day normally need no word for 'in'.
In the past, μπορώ (boró) shifts meaning: μπόρεσα (bóresa) = 'I managed to', not just 'I was able'. Δεν μπόρεσα να τελειώσω (dhen bóresa na telióso) = I didn't manage to finish.
Teachers split by school level: δασκάλα (dhaskála) = primary teacher; καθηγήτρια (kathiyítria) from secondary school up. Different jobs, different words.
Δεν... καθόλου (dhen... kathólou) = 'not... at all' – a stacked negative that's correct Greek: δεν μου αρέσει καθόλου (dhen mou arési kathólou).
